By leveraging a mix of virtualisation technologies and physical equipment, and including common software typically part of real-world organisations both open source and commercial, this proposal aims to achieve both the ability for the lab to scale to the size required for realistic evaluations as well as to include in the defined scenarios key elements often overlooked because of constraints of generalisation. Such laboratory will be instrumental particularly in measuring methodologies based on a data-driven approach and will enable to collect evidence on how such approach can steer the results towards removing the biases that affect traditional risk assessment practices based on estimations made by people involved in management and operations of processes and systems.

Ageing is a complex and natural biological process in which a series of physiological, morphological and biochemical alterations occur ubiquitously in tissues and organs (1). It is marked by a progressive decline in cellular and tissue functions where the underlying mechanisms, despite extensive studies, remain to be elucidated (2-3). An increase of genetic material instability, protein ANNEX B – Project Proposal Page 3 homeostatic loss and cellular senescence are the main causes of the most common age-related diseases such as neurodegeneration, cancer, chronic inflammation, cardiovascular diseases and musculoskeletal disorders (4). Concerning the musculoskeletal system, during ageing changes occur in bones, joints and muscles, which lead to the development of musculoskeletal related diseases. Between them, osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common degenerative joint disorder characterized by the gradual degeneration of all joint resulting in pain, joint stiffness and impaired movement, significantly reducing the quality of life for over 500 million people worldwide (4). OA is highly prevalent among the ageing population (5), often leads to joint pain, disability and a diminished quality of life (6).

CheckSig innovation is a software solution that implements a Covenant. CheckSig customizes the software of a Hardware Secure Module (HSM) improving the standard HSM security. 
customizing the software of a HSM improves the standard HSM security. The software customization:
A. constrains destination addresses to be defined in a previously established whitelist inside the HSM;
B. Enforces a requirement that the transaction must be authorized by a third party before the transaction can be signed using the HSM secret.  The third party cannot spend the bitcoin, but its authorization is required. 
The innovation reduces the risk of losing the bitcoins to an attacker that gets hold of the HSM, because the attacker cannot send the bitcoins to an address not in the whitelist, i.e. he cannot send the bitcoin to an address under his control.

Arboviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), West Nile virus (WNV) and Zika
virus (ZIKV) pose a global health threat and have spread in Europe due to climate change, immigration and
trade. Their persistence in human and non-human hosts has an impact on transmission dynamics and
complicates containment efforts. ZIKV, which is associated with congenital microcephaly, persists in various
human cells, crosses the blood-placental barrier and lingers in semen, leading to sexual transmission. The
mosquito-borne CHIKV, DENV and WNV occasionally persist in tissues in the post-acute phase. Tick-borne
encephalitis virus and Toscana virus also show persistence in humans, associated with chronic and worsening
disease. The mechanisms of persistence of arboviruses in humans, which are critical for viral evolution,
disease dynamics and public health, are poorly defined. GENESIS aims to comprehensively investigate the
molecular mechanisms of arbovirus replication and persistence and their interactions with the host and to
identify therapeutic targets.

Discovering properties which, for their own nature, can facilitate preparation and control of
quantum systems is of strategic importance for quantum science and technologies. The proposal fits into this context, in the spirit of Ilya Prigogine's idea that the complexity around us can be simplified when we deepen the description of the system.
It will delve into the exploitation of indistinguishability, a fundamental property of composite
quantum systems made of identical subsystems (particles of the same species, such as photons, atoms, electrons, nuclei). Extending previous results, we will investigate identical particle interferometry as an inherent resource for robust quantum state engineering and entanglement generation in complex networks, mitigating the environmental noise in quantum information tasks. The analysis, grounded on preliminary findings for two particles, will be generalized to many-particle systems to study scalability and robustness of the processes. The project will carry on the theoretical analysis and develop feasible proof-of-principle schemes to be realized in suited experimental platforms, such as quantum photonics and cavity-QED.

ECoN aims at studying and developing protocols of entanglement and nonlocality production,
characterization, quantification and activation in complex quantum networks (QNs), as well as
optimization strategies for their purification, distillation, routing, and distribution. It will investigate long-distance entanglement (LDE) preparation and detection in various instances of complex QNs, including: modular arrays of interlinked symmetry-protected topological chains and ladders, each featuring entangled edge modes; homogeneous and inhomogeneous arrays of quantum optical resonators driven by common entangling nonclassical fields; and linked stacks of surface (boundary) spins in homogeneous and inhomogeneous spin QNs. In parallel, ECoN will investigate the possibility of introducing: robust protocols for the generation of end-to-end entanglement at distance-independent rates in a complex QN; optimized schemes for its distribution across the network as a function of realistic network parameters such as entanglement routing probabilities, quantum memory characteristics, and gate fidelities; and protocols for entanglement purification in realistic conditions of noisy gates, depolarizing channels, and finite memory
storage times.

Arboviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), West Nile virus (WNV) and Zika
virus (ZIKV) pose a global health threat and have spread in Europe due to climate change, immigration and
trade. Their persistence in human and non-human hosts has an impact on transmission dynamics and
complicates containment efforts. ZIKV, which is associated with congenital microcephaly, persists in various
human cells, crosses the blood-placental barrier and lingers in semen, leading to sexual transmission. The
mosquito-borne CHIKV, DENV and WNV occasionally persist in tissues in the post-acute phase. Tick-borne
encephalitis virus and Toscana virus also show persistence in humans, associated with chronic and worsening
disease. The mechanisms of persistence of arboviruses in humans, which are critical for viral evolution,
disease dynamics and public health, are poorly defined. GENESIS aims to comprehensively investigate the
molecular mechanisms of arbovirus replication and persistence and their interactions with the host and to
identify therapeutic targets.

The proposal aims to deepen understanding of microbiota-vector interactions in phenomena related to i) environmental adaptation, ii) Insecticide resistance and iii) vectorial capacity of mosquitoes and iv) to fill the gap in  current knowledge of the sand fly microbiota. Both are vectors of several pathogenic viruses (Dengue, Chikungunya,  Zika, West Nile, Usutu). Global warming, extreme weather events and urbanization are favouring the spread of  invasive mosquito species such as us Aedes albopictus, Aedes koreicus and Aedes japonicus. Resistance to synthetic 
pyrethroids has recently been reported in Ae. albopictus populations across southern Europe. 
Vector microbiota likely influence multiple aspects of host biology, including vector competence, insecticide resistance and thermal adaptation; stable bacterial symbiosis is being used as an innovative mosquito control tool.

Quantum many-body batteries (QMBs) are systems described by the laws of quantum mechanics, which can be used to manage energy in nanoscale devices. They are made of qubits, which can exchange energy with a “bath”. In QMBs, collective effects play a pivotal role. In this proposal, we consider two solid-state platforms: circuit quantum electrodynamics architectures based on superconducting circuits and NV centers in diamond. In the first platform, one deals with transmons embedded in a low-loss cavity. In the second one, qubits are the NV centers in diamond, which can be manipulated e.g. via the application of classical external magnetic fields. NV centers are used for quantum sensing and have been proposed as systems for the realization of quantum memories. QMBs have two major objectives here. The first one is to use nonlinearities in superconducting circuits to realize QMBs displaying a genuine quantum advantage. Currently, indeed, the only QMBs where entanglement plays a key role in the charging dynamics are Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev batteries, which are difficult to realize experimentally. The second grand goal we have is to propose and study a multi-functional device based on NV centers in diamond, operating as a battery, memory, and cooperative sensor.

Arboviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), West Nile virus (WNV) and Zika
virus (ZIKV) pose a global health threat and have spread in Europe due to climate change, immigration and
trade. Their persistence in human and non-human hosts has an impact on transmission dynamics and
complicates containment efforts. ZIKV, which is associated with congenital microcephaly, persists in various
human cells, crosses the blood-placental barrier and lingers in semen, leading to sexual transmission. The
mosquito-borne CHIKV, DENV and WNV occasionally persist in tissues in the post-acute phase. Tick-borne
encephalitis virus and Toscana virus also show persistence in humans, associated with chronic and worsening
disease. The mechanisms of persistence of arboviruses in humans, which are critical for viral evolution,
disease dynamics and public health, are poorly defined. GENESIS aims to comprehensively investigate the
molecular mechanisms of arbovirus replication and persistence and their interactions with the host and to
identify therapeutic targets.
